newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Analysts view Australian wages jump with caution.
newsitem.headline: Analysts view Australian wages jump with caution.

text.p: Surprisingly strong Australian wages growth has deflated the prospects of a near term rate cut, but analysts were cautious about reading too much into the data as they said it may have been affected by public sector cutbacks.
Average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) rose 1.3 percent in the three months to February to be 4.6 percent higher over the previous 12 months, official data showed on Thursday.
The quarterly rise was the largest since May 1995, and the annual increase was the highest since the year to November 1995.

"They're pretty disappointing after all of the good news we've had on the wages and inflation outlook over the last couple of weeks -- the good outcome on the 'living wage', the good CPI numbers," Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said.
Market forecasts had centred on a 0.8 percent quarterly rise and a 4.3 percent annual rise.
Annual wages growth of 4.5 percent is seen as the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) "line in the sand" on wages, above which it becomes a threat to the maintenance of low inflation.
Apart from the possible implications for inflation, analysts also expressed some concern at the pace of wages growth given the unemployment rate had stalled above 8.5 percent.
"It must be a real concern to policy makers that we are getting such wage outcomes when the labour market is so weak," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
However, analysts were wary of over-reacting to the data, saying final wages data due on May 22, providing a split between public and private sector wages, may explain the growth.
In the year to last November, private sector wages grew by 2.8 percent while public sector wages surged 7.6 percent.
Private sector wages are seen as a more accurate reflection of the inflation pressures, as they are more likely to be seen in the prices of the goods and services those firms sell.

One factor, pointed to by the RBA, that may be influencing overall AWOTE growth was that if government cutbacks on public sector employment were mainly affecting lower paid workers, it would have the effect of lifting public sector AWOTE, even though such wage rises had not been granted.
In February, the RBA said if this was the case it may not be appropriate to draw strong conclusions from the data, and economists expressed similar views after the first quarter data.

"I wouldn't get overly concerned with that number," Bankers Trust senior economist David Bassanese said, adding the private/public split later this month was the key "because this number could be boosted by the distortions that are going on in the public sector."
However, as the RBA has warned that wages are the major threat to inflation, the data was enough to lengthen the odds on rates being cut following next week's RBA board meeting.
"Whatever reservations there might be with that number, it rules out a rate cut next week," HSBC Markets chief economist John Edwards said.

Instead a cut, which is still seen as only an outside chance by most analysts, would have to wait until at least the wages breakdown had become available, and maybe until another few months employment data were released.

"At this point in time you'd have to say that certainly a number like 4.6 percent is too high to be comfortable for the Reserve Bank, so basically forget any prospect of another cut in interest rates until it becomes clear that this is not a sign of accelerating wages growth," Dresdner's Henderson said.
